Hi! Hope you're doing well!

We're a team of Brazilian students: three of us are pursuing a BSc in Science and Technology, and one is studying Statistics. We're all really interested in science and research projects.

We always try to have fun, make the most of every experience, and learn something new along the way.

We also pay close attention to climate issues and are genuinely excited about this challenge!
summary:
When MODIS retires, 24 years of fire history could break in two. FireFly Lens keeps that record whole.

NASA’s two fire sensors describe the same fires differently. VIIRS has sharper 375 m pixels and reports about six times as many hot spots over Brazil as MODIS. Adding the two counts measures pixel size, not burning. We built a harmonization pipeline that writes the full record on the MODIS Aqua scale. It uses a negative binomial model trained on the 2018–2023 period when both sensors flew, by biome, month and day or night. On years held out from training, the bias of VIIRS against MODIS falls from 506% to under 1%, with a rank agreement of ρ = 0.99.

The result is a single fire calendar for South America from 2002 to today, in an interactive 3D map. Draw any area, or pick a state, city or country, and see its fire seasons month by month. Unusual months are flagged against the long-term median. A 3D time-lapse plays the seasons over the map. You can also ask our assistant, FireFlighter: “Show Espírito Santo between 2005 and 2012.” 

It’s open, validated and free to use, so firefighters, researchers and decision makers can compare 2002 with today. Our goal is not just to visualize fire detections, but to help people compare them responsibly across time.
details:
Repository: https://github.com/ThallesCansi/firefly-lens

Why we built it

We’re a team from Brazil, where the fire season shows up in the news, in the sky and sometimes in the air we breathe. When we read this challenge, one thing stood out. NASA’s two fire sensors, MODIS and VIIRS, describe the same fires in different ways. VIIRS sees the ground in sharper 375 m pixels, so over Brazil it reports about six times as many hot spots as MODIS. If you add the two, you measure pixel size, not fire. MODIS Aqua, which holds the longest record, is near the end of its mission. Without harmonization, 24 years of fire history could split into “before” and “after.”

We wanted to keep that history whole, and to make it accessible to everyone, not just people who work with satellite data. Beyond visualization, we wanted to give users scientific tools, meaningful metrics, and intuitive analyses to help them understand what the data reveals.

How it works

Our team consists of three undergraduate students in Science and Technology and one undergraduate student in Statistics. So, we started with the science. Our Python pipeline downloads real NASA FIRMS records: MODIS C6.1 Aqua and VIIRS 375 m NOAA-20. It keeps confident vegetation-fire detections and counts them on a 0.25° grid, by day and by day or night overpass. Between 2018 and 2023, both sensors flew side by side. Over that period, we trained a negative binomial model that learns how many MODIS hot spots each VIIRS detection stands for, by biome, month and time of day. The result is one continuous record on the MODIS Aqua scale. Through 2025, it uses MODIS as observed. From 2026 on, it uses VIIRS translated to the MODIS scale, with a 95% uncertainty range.

Next, we checked whether the model worked. On years held out from training, raw VIIRS read 506% above MODIS over Brazil. After harmonization, the bias was below 1%, and the ranking of the worst fire months matched almost perfectly (Spearman ρ = 0.99). Brazil is calibrated by biome. The 11 other South American countries are calibrated nationally, and each passed its own holdout tests.

Then we turned the numbers into something people can explore. FireFly Lens opens on a 3D globe over NASA Blue Marble imagery, with fire detections rising as columns. You can select an area in several ways: draw one, pick a state, city or country, or type coordinates. Then you can read the area’s fire history:

  • a month-by-year grid that flags unusual months against the 2003–2025 median;
  • a daily calendar that marks the fire season;
  • a time-lapse that plays the seasons over the map;
  • current weather-based fire danger indicators from NASA GFWED/GEOS-5 forecast products, based on the established Fire Weather Index (FWI) system. These indicators help users understand meteorological conditions favorable to fire, complementing the historical satellite record without claiming to predict exactly when or where fires will occur;
  • open the same area in NASA FIRMS Website.

You can download everything as CSV.

If you don’t want to click through menus, you can ask FireFlighter, our firefly mascot in a firefighter’s helmet. Type “Show Santa Catarina between 2005 and 2012” in any language. FireFlighter selects the state and sets the years, the user can then launch the time-lapse in the upper-right corner of the map. If the dates fall outside the record, it tells you what’s available. It answers only from the data and never makes up numbers.

Who it’s for and what we hope it changes

We picture someone in civil defense, a firefighter, a journalist, a teacher, or a student asking a simple question: “Is this fire season normal for my region?” Today, answering that can require GIS skills, extensive data cleaning, and statistical analysis. With FireFligther Lens, it takes just a few seconds to start exploring. Interactive charts, historical comparisons, and anomaly indicators help users look beyond the map, understand seasonal patterns, and put current fire activity into perspective. By bringing historical observations together with weather-based fire danger indicators, the platform also connects what has happened in the past with the conditions being monitored today. We hope this continuous, harmonized record supports more consistent and transparent fire research after MODIS retires, allowing observations from 2002 and 2026 to be compared on a common scale.

What we used

  • App: TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL for the 3D map, d3, Motion and KaTeX.
  • Science: Python with pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, statsmodels, Shapely and xarray.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS, NASA GFWED / GEOS-5, NASA GIBS, and boundaries from IBGE (the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics).
  • Assistant: Groq or Gemini models, called through a server route so that keys never reach the browser.
  • Hosting: Vercel. No special hardware is needed: everything runs in a browser, on a laptop or a phone.
  • AI use: we used AI coding assistants during development, and AI tools for parts of the presentation video.

What makes it different

Most fire maps show you a sea of dots. Some add calendars and charts. We wanted to go further, not just show where fires were detected, but give people the tools to investigate how fire activity has changed over more than two decades.

With FireFligther Lens, everything is connected and interactive. Users can explore a 3D map, select any region, navigate historical calendars, compare seasonal patterns, and investigate unusual periods through charts and statistical indicators. MODIS detections appear as rings and VIIRS as dots, while modeled periods are clearly distinguished from observed ones. And FireFlighter, our firefighter-helmeted mascot, helps users navigate these tools and understand the data without needing technical expertise.

But our biggest difference lies behind the interface. We didn't simply combine two satellite datasets. We implement a statistical method to make them comparable across time. Our dedicated scientific section opens up that process, with equations, references, validation results, uncertainty estimates, and documented limitations. We want users to explore the results, but also understand the science behind them.

We made its history something people can investigate.

What we cared about

  • Honesty: every estimate shows its uncertainty, the limits are documented on our Method page, and the app doesn’t show forecasts the data can’t support.
  • Accessibility: colorblind-safe colors, keyboard navigation, light and dark themes, and a mobile layout.
  • Speed and cost: the whole dataset is about 10 MB of static tiles, so it runs on free hosting and slow connections.
  • Respect for sources: NASA and every other data provider is credited. The project is not endorsed by NASA.
